why_them: They look after the Fulham Palace Oak, the roughly 500-year-old holm oak on the Bishop's Avenue lawn that we publish as lon_007 with an approved photograph.

org: The Honourable Society of the Inner Temple
why_them: The Inner Temple Mulberry on Benchers' Walk is one of our two Temple mulberry entries and we have no photograph of it.
The Hungry Tree, the London plane swallowing a cast-iron bench by their south gate on Constitution Hill, is the single most-viewed tree we publish in Dublin.
Two of Cork's five trees stand in their grounds: the Witch's Yew in the Rock Close and the great western red cedar.
Two of Cambridge's five trees are theirs, the Main Walk giant redwood and the hybrid Cambridge Oak by the Terrace Garden, and we hold no photograph of either.
They are the volunteer group restoring the Kings Weston estate landscape where our Oak of Kings Weston stands, and they map the estate's veteran trees themselves.
They run reserves and walks across the Bristol and Bath area we cover, including ground around Ashton Court where our Domesday Oak stands.
They coordinate the UK Tree Warden network, the volunteers most likely to know and photograph the individual trees we list in London, Bath, York, Bristol, Oxford and Cambridge.
Their Notable Trees work overlaps directly with our UK city lists, and their members are the people who actually measure and photograph trees like the Totteridge Yew.
They keep the Irish Champion Tree register that underpins several of our Dublin entries, including the Glasnevin tree of heaven we call Ireland's largest.

Seven of Edinburgh's fifteen trees stand in the Botanics, including the John Muir Grove of giant sequoias and the 1948 dawn redwood on the Chinese Hillside, and only two of those seven have a photograph.
They manage both the Royal Oak near Pen Ponds in Richmond Park and the Sweet Chestnut of Greenwich Park, two of the ten London trees we published first.

org: The Honourable Society of the Middle Temple (Estates)
why_them: The Fountain Court Mulberries are ours to describe and theirs to prune; we have no photograph of them and their estates team is the only one who can say which of the two is the older.

org: Trinity College Dublin, Estates and Facilities
why_them: Three Dublin entries are inside their walls: the Provost's Plane, the champion oriental planes of New Square and the last elm of College Park.
The Camperdown Elm in their churchyard below the Castle rock is one of our Edinburgh fifteen and has no photograph.
They hold three of our Irish entries: Queen Victoria's Sequoia at Aras an Uachtarain, the Great Sycamore of Farmleigh and the 1870 Campbell's magnolia in Fota Arboretum.
Their parks service runs St Anne's Park, where we publish both the many-trunked holm oak and the Holm Oak Avenue.
Corkagh Park in Clondalkin is theirs, and its oak avenue is the one Dublin entry that sits outside the city council's area.

org: National Botanic Gardens of Ireland, Glasnevin (OPW)
why_them: Six of Dublin's seventeen trees are theirs, from the Glasnevin dawn redwood to the tree of heaven we call Ireland's largest, and not one of the six has a photograph. Their own botanicgardens.ie returns 403 to our fetches, so the address was read on the OPW's Heritage Ireland page for the gardens.
The Totteridge Yew in their churchyard is the oldest living thing we publish in London and the tree that opens the London page.

org: City of London Corporation, City Gardens
why_them: Three City trees are on their ground and all three lack a photograph: the Cheapside Plane, the Finsbury Circus pagoda tree and the planes in St Paul's north churchyard.
The Bobart Yew of 1645 in their Walled Garden is our only photographed Oxford tree, and their white mulberry beside it still has no picture.
Veteran trees are their whole subject and several of ours are textbook cases for them, including the hollow Darnley Sycamore in Glasgow and the Cammo Ash in Edinburgh.
Urban trees in exactly our cities are their work, and our London page now runs to 23 street and square trees, from the Amwell Street fig to the Marylebone elm.

org: National Trust, Prior Park Landscape Garden
why_them: The Yews of Prior Park near the Sham Bridge are one of Bath's five entries and we have no photograph of them.

org: London Borough of Hammersmith and Fulham, Cleaner and Greener
why_them: Ravenscourt Park gives us two London entries, the Baobab Plane and the tree of heaven, and neither has a photograph.

He writes about London's street trees tree by tree, which is precisely what our London page does for the Amwell Street fig, the Dorchester plane and the Marylebone elm; his site publishes no address, only a Jetpack contact form.
All six York trees stand in their Museum Gardens, including the cut-leaved hornbeam and the pear-barked beech, and we also run a separate park page for the gardens.

org: The City of Edinburgh Council, Parks and Greenspace
why_them: Four Edinburgh entries are on council ground: the Cammo Ash, the monkey puzzles of Lauriston Castle, the Cramond rockface sycamore and the beeches of the Hermitage of Braid. Their site renders every address in JavaScript, so nothing could be verified; customer.care@edinburgh.gov.uk is published on their contact page but is a general switchboard.

org: Glasgow City Council, Parks and Open Spaces
why_them: Three of Glasgow's four trees are theirs: the Darnley Sycamore, the Suffragette Oak in Kelvingrove Park and the King's Park yews. Every page on glasgow.gov.uk returns a JavaScript shell, so no address could be read.

org: Bath and North East Somerset Council, Parks
why_them: Royal Victoria Park holds two of Bath's five trees, the Caucasian elm at the Royal Avenue entrance and the coast redwood in the Great Dell, and neither has a photograph. Their site renders contact details in JavaScript, so no address could be verified.

The Milton Mulberry in their Fellows' Garden, planted in 1608, is one of only two Cambridge trees we have a photograph of, and they are the only people who can confirm its condition. Their contact page publishes a form and phone numbers, no address.

org: University College Cork, Buildings and Estates
why_them: Two of Cork's five trees are on their campus, the Boole Library redwoods and the Monterey pine at the Western Road gates, and both lack a photograph. The estates pages return an empty 833-byte shell; ucc.ie's contact index lists departmental addresses but none for estates.

The Craigmillar Castle Yews are ours to describe and theirs to manage, and they are the only Edinburgh castle tree with an approved photograph. Every page on their site is JavaScript-rendered, so no address could be read.

org: National Trust for Scotland, Holmwood House
why_them: Holmwood's giant redwoods are one of only four Glasgow entries and have no photograph. nts.org.uk serves a 5KB JavaScript shell on every page, so no address could be verified.
